objectives.text: Recover the Chagos Archipelago, Diego Garcia included, through the treaty signed with the UK on 22 May 2025: sovereignty to Mauritius, with a 99-year lease of the base back to London. Ratification has stalled: the Bill ran out of time in the Lords, London has accepted that US consent cannot be secured for now, and the handover was shelved in April 2026.

paradoxes.text: The treaty that would return the islands needs the consent of the power that wants the base kept. Port Louis signed a deal that Washington now blocks, and the ties it builds with India and China give it leverage elsewhere, not in Washington.

grand_strategy.reading: Mauritius wants the Chagos back and has the 2025 treaty as its best instrument, but ratification now waits on a US consent that Washington withholds and that London has accepted it cannot secure for now. Meanwhile Port Louis plays the two Asian powers against each other for money and security, India through funding and an enhanced partnership, China through a loan and a free trade agreement, without an alliance with either. The test is whether London and Washington rework the deal in a form Port Louis can sign, and whether the Safe City questions at home cost the government room to negotiate.

stances.note: Partner with grievance. The 22 May 2025 treaty makes London and Port Louis counterparts on the islands, but it is unratified and creates no alignment, so the grade stays partner. The grievance is the British claim to the Chagos that the treaty would end. Trend cooling: the Bill ran out of time in the Lords and the handover was shelved in April 2026; in September 2026 Trump called the deal 'terrible', and the UK said it would revisit the deal with the annual payments on hold. Bond grievance is the structure under the posture. Confidence B: one tier 2 source (Chatham House) plus tier 3 reporting; the UK card's row toward MUS is mirrored here with the same sources.

stances.note: Claimed, not controlled. Mauritius claims the whole Chagos Archipelago, Diego Garcia included, while the UK administers it and the base is used by the UK and US. Diego Garcia is graded inside that claim, not as own territory: the treaty would pass sovereignty to Mauritius, but with the base leased back to the UK for 99 years, so even on the treaty's own terms Port Louis would not control the base; own_territory would apply only to the rest of the archipelago once the handover took effect, and only after ratification. The since date is the 2025 treaty, the earliest dated source; the claim itself is older. Trend stable: the claim is restated in the treaty and in the 2026 shelving, not withdrawn. Bond grievance: an open wound the treaty is meant to close. Confidence B: one tier 2 source (Chatham House) plus tier 3 reporting.

stances.note: Partner, not ally: the state visit of 11-12 March 2025 upgraded ties to an 'enhanced strategic partnership' with eight agreements, a framework rather than a treaty of alliance. India funded the Agalega airstrip and jetty (opened by video link in February 2024); Mauritius says it is no base, and local protests read it as a sovereignty cost. Warming because the partnership was upgraded in 2025 and the cooperation list is wide (maritime security, local-currency trade). Bond affinity: a shared Indian Ocean position and close ties, no treaty kinship; Modi's 'family' language is not counted as kin. stances.note: Transactional. Diplomatic relations date from the joint communique of 15 April 1972. The free trade agreement (in force 1 January 2021) and the 2018 China Eximbank buyer's credit of US$73.7m for the Safe City system bind the two governments through money, not alignment. Safe City is under parliamentary questioning (March 2025), and Mauritius was one of three states that revoked overflight for Taiwan's president in April 2026, which Taipei blames on Chinese pressure (Taiwan card, unverified by Beijing or Port Louis): a cooperative reading, not a partnership of values. Trend stable: the FTA and credit point to warming, the scrutiny of Safe City to cooling. Bond none: no kinship and no open grievance.

stances.note: Partner, no treaty. Diplomatic relations date from 12 March 1968 (US State Department record; the access date recorded by Wikipedia's citation is 2023-07). The US is the decisive actor on Chagos: it uses the base and it has not given the consent the UK says the handover needs. Trump called the deal a 'terrible deal' on 22 September 2026, the UK shelved ratification in April 2026 under US pressure, and US Senator Kennedy urged the King in April 2026 to protect the base. Trend stable: Port Louis has not moved against Washington; the cooling is Washington's, not Mauritius's. Bond none: no shared identity and no grievance aimed at the US itself. Confidence B: a tier 1 record of the relation, tier 3 reporting on the posture.

Not ratified: the Bill passed the Commons (318-174) but ran out of time in the Lords by April 2026, no ratification Bill is planned for the next King's Speech, and the government has accepted that US consent cannot be secured for now; Trump called the deal 'an act of great stupidity'. The government's June 2026 letter says it remains 'confident' in the deal.

relations_to.summary: After the 2025 Chagos treaty stalled in Parliament and in Washington's eyes, Trump told Burnham at their first meeting in New York on 22 Sep 2026 that he thought the Chagos deal 'terrible'. On 23 Sep Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that Trump's position on the deal 'as currently drafted' was not changing and that the government had to do more work with the US to bring the deal to a place it could support. Reported as a rework rather than an abandonment.
